name: Galway Cathedral
label: Galway Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Salmon Weir Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Salmon Weir Bridge' (way/1024339556): middle (84 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/150786580: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galway Cathedral' (109 m across).
notes: Large domed cathedral beside the River Corrib.

text.description:
Galway Cathedral is the big limestone landmark on Nun's Island, with a green dome that shows above the rooftops and the river. Building started in 1958 on the site of the old Galway Gaol and finished in 1965. It is often described as the last great stone cathedral built in Europe. The architect was John J. Robinson. The dome and pillars follow a Renaissance style, and the rose windows and mosaics draw on wider Christian art. The dome stands 44.2 metres high, which is why it is easy to spot across the city.

Guides call this the classic postcard view. The cathedral rises from Nun's Island with the River Corrib and the bridge in the foreground, so you get the whole building and some water in one frame. The stone is a pale, even colour, so the green dome stands out well against the sky.

For a second view, try the pedestrian bridge beside Salmon Weir Bridge. It frames the cathedral from closer range, with the canal and water in front. Check the map before you go to find it. The cathedral is an active place of worship, so don't photograph services and don't use flash inside.
text.geographic_location: Galway Cathedral stands on Nun's Island, beside the River Corrib. The Salmon Weir Bridge viewpoint is on the river beside it.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops at this spot, so head for Galway city centre and continue to the River Corrib. Walk to Salmon Weir Bridge and stand on it, looking west towards the cathedral. From the bridge it is about 2 minutes on foot to the cathedral itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) on the bridge to fit the dome, the building and some river in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for the dome and its details. Only use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move to the closer pedestrian bridge and the cathedral won't fit otherwise.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Salmon Weir Bridge. The cathedral's green domed exterior rising from Nun's Island, with the river and the bridge in the foreground. From there the green dome rises from Nun's Island, with the Corrib and the bridge in the foreground. Pick a spot where the parapet or railing doesn't cut across the cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water in the bottom third and the dome near the upper line. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. If the crowd or traffic is in the way, try the pedestrian bridge beside the bridge for a closer view across the canal.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. If the river is calm, a Live Photo can catch small ripples in the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A quiet morning or around sunset, when the dome catches the changing light.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public bridge, but the cathedral is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements, and avoid photographing services.

name: Spanish Arch
label: Spanish Arch
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nimmo's Pier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Nimmo's Pier' (way/131880810): point nearest the subject (213 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/36783334: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spanish Arch' (40 m across).
notes: Historic arch beside the River Corrib and the Long Walk.

text.description:
The Spanish Arch is a short stretch of old stonework beside the River Corrib in Galway. Two arches survive here, the Spanish Arch and the Caoċ ("blind") Arch. They are what remains of a wall built in 1584, in the mayoralty of Wylliam Martin, to protect the city's quays. The "Spanish" name is not as old as the stonework. In the 18th century the Eyre family extended the quays and made the arches to give the town access to them. The 1755 tsunami from the Lisbon earthquake partly destroyed them. Until 2006 part of the structure housed Galway City Museum, which now has its own building just behind.

This view is not taken at the arch itself. You shoot it from Nimmo's Pier, along the pier beside the Claddagh Quay. From there the arch sits across the water, with boats and the surrounding buildings in the frame, so it reads as part of the waterfront rather than a lone monument. It suits a wide photo: leave some water in the foreground and let the buildings frame the sides.

If you want the stone close up, walk over to the arch afterwards. There the arch fills the foreground and the Claddagh shoreline and Galway Bay open out behind it. South Park gives a broader panorama that places the arch in the Claddagh area and the bay. Cobbles can be slippery after rain and spray can reach the quay, so wipe your lens now and then.
text.geographic_location: The Spanish Arch is on the bank of the River Corrib in Galway city centre, beside the Long Walk promenade and just in front of Galway City Museum.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from Galway city centre and go to Nimmo's Pier beside the Claddagh Quay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view across the water. If the arch looks too small, tap 2x or more on a telephoto lens to bring it closer, and avoid the ultra-wide (0.5x) unless you want a lot of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nimmo's Pier (along the pier beside the Claddagh Quay). The arch seen from a distance across the water, with boats and surrounding buildings in the frame for a wide shot. From here you see the arch at a distance across the water, with boats and nearby buildings in the shot. The arch is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch on one of the third lines, with boats or the water edge as foreground. Keep the horizon level and include the neighbouring buildings to show the setting. For a different angle, the Spanish Arch itself gives the stone in the foreground with Galway Bay behind, and South Park gives a panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Wipe the lens first if there has been spray.

text.access_note: Some details may be a few years old, so check current access before you go.

name: Eyre Square
label: Eyre Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quincentennial Fountain' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quincentennial Fountain' (node/1874242427): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25192080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Eyre Square' (211 m across).
notes: Central city park with the Browne Doorway and fountain.

text.description:
Eyre Square is a rectangular public park in the middle of Galway, right in the city centre, next to the shopping streets of William Street and Shop Street. It began as a medieval green in front of a town gate and was given to the city in 1710 by Mayor Edward Eyre, who gave it his name. The west side was pedestrianised when the square reopened on 13 April 2006. John F. Kennedy made a speech here on 29 June 1963, and a bust of him stands in the park.

For photographs, the Quincentennial Fountain at the northern end is the easiest starting point. Its bronze hooker-boat sculpture makes a strong foreground, with the open square and shopfronts behind it, and it ties the square to Galway's maritime heritage. Guides call it the most photographed feature here. For a second picture, walk to the Browne Doorway on the east side. It is a carved stone doorway that was moved to the square in 1905 from a Browne family home on Lower Abbeygate Street. Frame it from the lawns or paving so the trees and open space show around it. In the north section you may also spot the banners of the fourteen Tribes of Galway, which add colour to a wider shot.

The square gets busy. Street performers are often about, so ask before photographing one person. The Christmas market (November to January, with a Big Wheel) and festival events can block views and crowd the fountain.
text.geographic_location: Eyre Square is in Galway city centre, next to the William Street and Shop Street shopping area. Galway railway station is right beside it.
text.directions_text: Eyre Square sits at the edge of Galway's main shopping streets, so from Shop Street or William Street you can simply walk to it. Galway railway station is adjacent, so arriving by train puts you at the edge of the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain and its bronze boat. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole open square and the shopfronts behind. Use 2x on the telephoto for a closer, tidier view of the Browne Doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (northern end of the square). The fountain's bronze hooker-boat sculpture in the foreground, with the open square and surrounding shopfronts behind it. At the northern end of the square. From here the bronze hooker-boat sculpture is in the foreground, and the open square and surrounding shopfronts spread out to the south behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the boat sculpture on one of the lower third points, leaving the open square and shopfronts behind it. Crouch slightly to lift the boat against the background. For a second picture, go to the Browne Doorway on the east side and frame it from the lawns or paving, with trees and open space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the boat sculpture to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the bronze keeps its detail. If the Browne Doorway is behind plexiglass, hold the phone close to the glass and angle it slightly to cut reflections. If people walk through your shot, try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, for warm light and reflections on the fountain water. Early in the day is likely to be quieter. Expect crowds and blocked views during the Christmas market and festival events.

text.access_note: Eyre Square is an open public park in the city centre; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit during the Christmas market or a festival, when the square may be busy and views blocked.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is likely to be quieter in the square.
Holding the phone close to the glass and angling it slightly can reduce reflections on the plexiglass around the Browne Doorway.
Street performers are often about, and it is polite to ask before photographing one person.
The stand-here point is about 1 minute on foot from the middle of the square (39 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).

name: Shop Street
label: Shop Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eyre Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Eyre Square' (way/25192080): middle (210 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25039799: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Shop Street' (83 m long).
notes: Lively pedestrian street with buskers and colourful shopfronts.

text.description:
Shop Street is Galway's main shopping street and the busy heart of the old centre. It has been pedestrianised since the late 1990s, so you can stop and frame a shot without traffic. Old brick buildings, bright shopfronts and plenty of pubs line the way, and street performers and buskers are a regular sight. Lynch's Castle stands on the street. This 16th-century building is one of central Galway's best preserved historic buildings, and it became a bank branch in the 1960s. It is worth a frame of its own.

The street photographs well because so much colour and detail is packed into a narrow space. From there you can take a wider view of the square with its historic and modern buildings, and the start of Shop Street at the edge of the frame. Then walk down into the street for close-up shots of shopfronts, pub signs and cobbles. If you want another angle, the narrow street curving up towards St. Nicholas' Collegiate Church makes a nice alternative, with stonework in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: Shop Street is in the middle of Galway's old centre, running west from Eyre Square. Eyre Square is officially John F. Kennedy Memorial Park.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from Eyre Square, the open green at the east end of the street, and walk south-west into Shop Street. Eyre Square is the easiest place to start; check local transport options for getting into central Galway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) on Eyre Square for the open view. In the street itself, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the shopfronts and signs running away from you. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for details such as pub signs and carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Eyre Square (the open green at the east end of Shop Street, where the street begins). A wider open-air view of the square and the surrounding historic and modern buildings, with the start of Shop Street at the edge of the frame. The open green at the east end of Shop Street. From here your photo shows a wider open-air view of the square and the surrounding historic and modern buildings, with the start of Shop Street at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the start of Shop Street on one of the side lines, so the buildings of the square fill the rest of the frame. Once you are in the street, keep the cobbles in the lower third and let the shopfronts lead the eye down the lane. For a different view, try the curve of the narrow street towards St. Nicholas' Collegiate Church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a shopfront to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich. If you want a close-up of a busker, ask first. A Live Photo can catch a little of the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you want fewer people in the frame, as the street is busiest when shoppers are about.

text.access_note: Shop Street is an open, fully pedestrianised public street and Eyre Square is a free, open public park, though it is worth checking local signs for any temporary works.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the street is likely to be quieter, with fewer people in the frame.
The street is busiest when shoppers are about.
Bright skies can make shopfront colours look washed out, so lowering the exposure slider helps.

name: Salthill
label: Salthill Promenade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Blackrock Diving Tower' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Blackrock Diving Tower' (way/954629497): middle (27 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1856447860: the OpenStreetMap point 'Salthill'.

text.description: Salthill is Galway's seaside district, and its best-known photo subject is the Blackrock Diving Tower: a yellow concrete tower standing out in open water on Galway Bay. It was built in 1953 and is still used by swimmers and divers, so you will often see people on the platform, which adds scale and life to a picture. Each Christmas Day people traditionally jump from it into the sea, raising money for local charities. The tower sits on the Salthill promenade, known locally as "the Prom" (Irish: Bóthar na Trá). The promenade is about 2 km long and opened in 1856. The tower photographs well because its bright colour stands out against the grey-blue water and the sky, and the waves breaking around its base add movement. From the promenade you can also take a wider view of Galway Bay, with the Burren hills visible across the water. For a closer shot, walk to a spot a little to the south of the tower, on the rocks or sand, with the Atlantic and Galway Bay behind it. The tide changes the look of the scene, so a second visit at a different time can give a different picture. Keep a safe distance from wet, exposed rocks, especially in stormy weather, when the waves around the tower can be dangerous.
text.geographic_location: Salthill is a seaside area to the south-west of Galway city centre, overlooking Galway Bay. The Blackrock Diving Tower stands at the water's edge by the promenade.
text.directions_text: From Galway city centre, Bus Éireann route 401 runs from Eyre Square to Salthill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) or ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wider view of Galway Bay and plenty of sky. If you walk closer to the tower, 1x shows the whole tower against the open bay, and 0.5x adds the waves at the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (shoot from the rocks or sand to the south of the tower, with the Atlantic and Galway Bay behind it). The yellow concrete diving tower standing against open water of Galway Bay, often with swimmers or divers on the platform. From here you get a wider view of Galway Bay, with the tower in the distance, so use telephoto for the tower itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving open water and sky around it. From where you stand, include the curve of the coastline and the Burren hills across the bay, with the tower small in the distance. Walk closer: for a bigger view of the tower, go to the rocks or sand just south of it, with the Atlantic and Galway Bay behind it, and crouch a little so the waves at the base sit in the lower part of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the yellow does not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch waves breaking and people jumping. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray can leave marks on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun lights the side of the tower. Sunset is also a good time. Check the tide, which changes the water around the base and the reflections.

text.access_note: The tower and promenade are in open public space, but check local signs and conditions before you go, and keep away from exposed rocks in rough weather.
claims_not_in_sources: Sea spray can leave marks on a phone lens, so it is worth wiping it before shooting.
The yellow of the tower can look washed out in bright light, so lowering the exposure helps.
The walk from the Blackrock Diving Tower to the stand-here point is roughly 15–20 minutes.

name: Galway City Museum
label: Galway City Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/10028843150: the OpenStreetMap point 'Galway City Museum'.
notes: Museum next to the Spanish Arch.

text.description:
Galway City Museum is a modern, L-shaped building beside the River Corrib, right next to the Spanish Arch. It was designed by Ciaran O'Connor and Ger Harvey of the Office of Public Works, and it won the Bank of Ireland Opus Architectural Award in 2006. The architects kept it to three levels so it would sit comfortably with the older buildings around it. That restrained height helps your photos, because the whole building fits in the frame without any tricks.

The design also leaves an open plaza between the museum and the Spanish Arch. Here you can combine a contemporary building with a piece of the medieval town wall in one picture. The Arch is a protected monument that was once part of the defences around Galway. The plaza is a public space and is sometimes used for civic events.

The present building opened in April 2007, behind the site of the earlier museum at Comerford House, which closed in 2004. Inside are collections on Galway's history, including medieval carved stones, items from the Claddagh and a statue of Pádraic Ó Conaire.

For photos, step back across the plaza so the building and the Arch share the frame. Keep your phone level using the gridlines, and take a few close-ups of the building's edges and surfaces as well as the wide view.
text.geographic_location: In Galway City, on the bank of the River Corrib beside the Spanish Arch. The museum's plaza lies between the two.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Spanish Arch beside the River Corrib. The museum is next to it. Once there, the phone icon on the map is right at the museum. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the building and the open plaza together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk a few steps back onto the plaza between the museum and the Spanish Arch to fit more of the building into your photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the museum's vertical edges up with them so the walls don't lean. Try one frame with the museum and the Spanish Arch together to show old and new side by side. Take another close-up of the building's surfaces using 2x zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and washing out the picture. Check the edges of the frame when using 0.5x, as buildings can look stretched near the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the plaza is usually quieter.

text.access_note: The plaza outside is a public space, but check the official site before you go for museum entry and any rules on photography inside.

name: Claddagh
label: Claddagh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Long Walk' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of The Long Walk nearest the subject (our map tiles).
notes: Historic fishing village at the mouth of the Corrib, home of the Claddagh ring.

text.description:
The Claddagh (An Cladach, meaning 'the seashore') sits close to the centre of Galway, where the River Corrib meets Galway Bay. It was once a fishing village just outside the old city walls, and locals supplied the city with seafood from the fish market by the Spanish Arch, just across the river. The original thatched cottages were cleared in the 1930s and replaced by council housing, so today's scene is a lived-in neighbourhood rather than a museum piece. The area is also the birthplace of the Claddagh ring, with its two clasped hands holding a crowned heart.

The best photo is taken from the Long Walk on the east bank of the Corrib, looking west across the water. From there you see the row of coloured houses on the Claddagh side, often framed with their reflection in the river. Guides treat it as the classic postcard angle, and it is quieter than the city centre, especially early or late in the day.

On a phone, keep the composition simple. Put the houses along the lower third of the frame and let the water and sky fill the rest. If the river is calm, include plenty of water so the reflection becomes part of the picture. If you have time, Claddagh Basin makes a good second stop, with swans and the Spanish Arch across the water. Remember that people live here, so stay on public paths and be considerate when photographing the houses.
text.geographic_location: The Claddagh is on the west side of the River Corrib, where the river meets Galway Bay, just across from the Spanish Arch and a short way from the city centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stops are listed for this spot. From there the Claddagh houses are about 230 m to the west, across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole row of houses and their reflection. If you want to pick out the houses and leave out the buildings around them, try 2x or 3x if your phone has it. The ultra-wide (0.5x) takes in more sky and water, but it makes the houses look small and can stretch the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Long Walk (east bank of the Corrib, facing west across the water). The row of coloured houses on the Claddagh side, usually framed with its reflection in the river. On the east bank of the Corrib, and face west across the water. Stay on the public path and keep out of the way of people walking past.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the water's edge up with the lower third, so the houses sit in a straight band and the reflection fills the foreground. Keep your phone level so the houses don't lean. Move a few steps along the bank to avoid lamp posts and railings. If you have time, Claddagh Basin is a quieter alternative, with the swans and the Spanish Arch across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the houses don't turn pale. Hold the phone with both hands, as the footing along the river can be narrow in places. A Live Photo can catch ripples on the water, but check the reflection afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend early morning or golden hour. These are also the quietest times.

text.access_note: The Long Walk is an open public riverside path, but the Claddagh is a residential area, so stay on public paths and respect residents' privacy.

name: Lynch's Castle
label: Lynch's Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shop Street' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q140606158: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Medieval town house with gargoyles on Shop Street.

text.description:
Lynch's Castle is a fortified townhouse on Shop Street in the middle of Galway. It was built by the Lynch family, one of the Tribes of Galway, and is thought to date from the 15th or early 16th century. It is one of only two surviving fortified town houses in the city that belonged to the Tribes, the other being Blake's Castle. Today it works as a branch of AIB, so it looks like a bank on the ground floor and a medieval townhouse above.

It photographs well because the limestone front is full of detail: carved stonework, coats of arms (including that of King Henry VII) and a corner turret. The building was once five storeys tall. The floor levels were altered in 1820 and Georgian windows were added. The bank took over the premises in the early 20th century, and the building has been AIB's since 1966.

The best view is from the pavement directly opposite, across Shop Street. From there the whole carved front fits in one frame, along with both faces of the corner turret. Shop Street is lively, with crowds and street buskers, so an early visit gives you a clearer view. The street scene around the building is part of the picture, so you don't need to crop it out. If you want a second angle, try the corner of Shop Street and Abbeygate Street (check the exact street name on the day), where you can see the side of the building as well as the front.
text.geographic_location: Lynch's Castle stands on Shop Street in the centre of Galway city, at the corner with Abbeygate Street. The cross street may be named differently, so check the exact corner on the day.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop information for this spot, so simply head for Shop Street in the middle of Galway city centre. The castle is at a corner with Abbeygate Street (check the exact street on the day). Once you are on Shop Street, cross to the pavement opposite the building, which is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street, which shows the building much as the eye sees it. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole front and turret, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the carved coats of arms and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is the castle itself, so cross Shop Street and stand on the pavement directly opposite the façade. From here the full limestone front, the carved stonework, the coats of arms and the corner turret all sit in one frame with the street around them. For a different view, walk to the corner of Shop Street and Abbeygate Street (check the exact street name on the day) to see the second face of the corner tower and the side of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Face the building squarely so both sides of the corner turret are visible. Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the walls with them to keep the verticals straight. Include a little of the street at the bottom to give a sense of place, and wait for a gap in the crowd if you can. The corner with Abbeygate Street gives a good second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the carving keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning, when one visitor guide says the limestone photographs best. An early start gives you fewer crowds and buskers.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed freely from the street, but the building is a working AIB bank and the interior is not open for touring, so check the official site before you go if you want to see more.
claims_not_in_sources: The pavement opposite may be too narrow to fit the whole front in the default lens (1x), so ultra-wide may help.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.
Exposure may need lowering if the sky is bright.

name: Long Walk, Galway
label: Long Walk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Claddagh Quay' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Claddagh Quay nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W34707194 (The Long Walk): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Row of colourful houses along the Corrib by the Spanish Arch.

text.description:
The Long Walk is the row of colourful houses that runs along the water's edge beside the River Corrib, with the city's historic core rising up behind it. It photographs well because the bright façades, the open water and the old town sit in one frame, with nothing in the way.

The best angle is from the opposite bank, on the Claddagh side, at Claddagh Quay. From there you see the whole row at once, with the river in the foreground. Guides call this the classic view, and most of the well-known photos of the row are taken from here. If you have time for only one spot, make it this one.

If you want a second angle, Nimmo's Pier gives a view back across the water toward the houses, with boats and the river in the frame. The Spanish Arch shows the full line of houses stretching away along the quay.

The Long Walk is a row of private homes, so stay on the public quay and don't go onto the properties. Keep the water in the lower part of the picture and let the houses fill the middle. Early morning or late afternoon is said to bring out the colours of the façades best. If you arrive by car, check the parking signs carefully first, as one visitor reports clampers on the road.
text.geographic_location: The Long Walk is in Galway city, beside the historic core, on the River Corrib. It lies on the opposite bank from Claddagh Quay and the Claddagh side, which is where the best view is taken.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stops serve this spot. The best view is from Claddagh Quay on the Claddagh side, opposite the row. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start at 1x and step back or switch lenses if the whole row doesn't fit, keeping the water in front. Try 2x if you want a tighter picture of the façades without the empty sky. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Claddagh Quay (opposite bank, on the Claddagh side of the Corrib). The whole row of colourful houses along the Long Walk, with the water in the foreground and the city's historic core behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the water's edge up with the lower grid line, so the houses sit in the middle band. Keep the phone level so the row doesn't lean. For a different view, Nimmo's Pier looks back across the water with boats in the frame, and the Spanish Arch gives a long view along the quay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. A Live Photo can catch movement on the water, and you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is warmest on the façades.

text.access_note: The quay is a public space, but the Long Walk houses are private homes, so stay on the public quay and check parking signs before you leave a car.

name: St. Nicholas' Collegiate Church
label: St Nicholas' Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lombard Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lombard Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/128910161: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Saint Nicholas' (66 m across).
notes: Medieval church said to be visited by Columbus.

text.description:
St Nicholas' Collegiate Church is a medieval church in the middle of Galway. It was founded in 1320 and dedicated to Saint Nicholas of Myra, the patron saint of seafarers, which suits a port town. In 1484 it became a collegiate church, the same year Galway received its royal charter and mayoral status. Local legend says Christopher Columbus worshipped here in 1477, though that is a story rather than a proven fact. The church is still in use today for worship, including by several different congregations.

It photographs well because the tower and the old stonework tell the story of the building without any help. A Galway travel guide recommends Lombard Street for the exterior, because the tower and the weathered stone fit into one frame. The church sits in a narrow medieval lane, so a wide shot of the whole building can be hard to get at street level. Take your time, and try a tall frame that runs from the stonework up to the tower. Market Street also gives a view of the outside, and the Church Yard Lane entrance is good for the vaulted south porch and the doorway.
text.geographic_location: St Nicholas' Collegiate Church stands in the centre of Galway city, in a narrow medieval lane.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Galway city centre and head for Lombard Street on foot. For the south porch, walk round to the Church Yard Lane entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the tower and the stonework together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane is too tight for 1x, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lombard Street. The church's exterior with its tower and medieval stonework in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright so the stonework and the tower fit in one tall frame, and switch on gridlines to keep the tower straight. Tilting the phone upwards makes the walls lean inwards, so hold it level and step back if you can. For a different view, try Market Street, or the Church Yard Lane entrance for the vaulted south porch and doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Wipe your lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter in a narrow lane, and softer light is kinder to old stone. Services may be in progress, so it is worth planning around them.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship and photography inside is generally allowed, but services may be in progress, so check the official site before you go.

name: Salmon Weir Bridge
label: Salmon Weir Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Droichead an Dóchais' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Droichead an Dóchais' (way/1054895448): middle (53 m across); moved 25 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1024339556: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Salmon Weir Bridge' (84 m across).
notes: Bridge over the Corrib with views of the cathedral.

text.description:
Salmon Weir Bridge carries traffic and pedestrians across the River Corrib in the middle of Galway, with the weir running beside it and Galway Cathedral's dome rising above the trees on the far bank. That mix of old stone, fast water and a big landmark is why it photographs so well. The bridge was designed by William Vitruvius Morrison to link the new Courthouse with the new Gaol on Nun's Island, and it was first known as the Gaol Bridge. Its foundation stone was laid on 29 June 1818 and it opened in October 1819. It is on Galway City Council's Record of Protected Structures.

It is on Droichead an Dóchais, the newer pedestrian and cycle bridge that runs alongside the original. From this parallel deck you look across at the older stone bridge with the Cathedral behind it. Guides suggest it as a quieter alternative to the busier view from the old bridge itself, and there is seating here with a good view of the Cathedral. The older bridge itself gives the classic view of the river tumbling over the weir with the dome above the trees, so it is worth a second shot if you have time. If you want a salmon photo, check the run dates on the day. The Corrib can be dangerous in flood, so keep to the marked walkways.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Galway city, where the River Corrib passes the weir beside Nun's Island, with Galway Cathedral on the far bank.
text.directions_text: Head for Nun's Island in Galway city. Droichead an Dóchais runs alongside the old bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the old bridge, the water and the Cathedral together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole deck and railings in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Droichead an Dóchais (the new pedestrian and cycle bridge, alongside the original bridge). The older stone bridge and the Cathedral seen from a parallel deck, giving a less crowded angle on the same scene. From here the older stone bridge and the Cathedral appear side by side, with the old bridge to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the old bridge's arches along a lower line, with the Cathedral dome near an upper third. Keep the phone level so the parapets stay straight. For a different view, try the old Salmon Weir Bridge itself, looking at the river over the weir with the dome above the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the bridge. Soft, even light usually suits the stonework and the water. Check the salmon run dates if you hope to photograph fish.

text.access_note: Droichead an Dóchais and the old bridge are open public crossings, but stay on the walkways and take care near the water; check the official site before you go if in doubt.

name: Blake's Castle
label: Blake's Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quay Street' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Medieval tower house near the quays.

text.description: Blake's Castle is a narrow medieval tower house on Quay Street, in the middle of Galway city. It was built around 1470 and first belonged to the O'Halloran family. The Blake family fortified it in 1641. From 1686 to 1810 it served as the county gaol. Later it stored corn, and it was then left to fall derelict. In 1993 a hotel opened beside it, and the hotel's design incorporated the castle's façade, so the old stonework now stands at the foot of the street. It is also one of only two surviving fortified town houses in Galway owned by the Tribes of Galway, the other being Lynch's Castle. It photographs well because the tall, slim tower fills the end of the street, with its corner windows and rooftop parapet clearly visible. Standing on the pavement, you can take it straight on and still show the street around it, which gives a sense of how an old fortified house sits among modern buildings. It is a quick stop. Allow a few minutes to try a wide shot and a closer one of the top. Keep an eye on passing people and traffic, and step back to the kerb edge only where it is safe. The façade is part of the hotel, so check the hotel's official site for access details.
text.geographic_location: Blake's Castle is on Quay Street in Galway city centre, built into the frontage beside the hotel at the lower end of the street.
text.directions_text: Head for Quay Street in Galway city centre; the castle stands at the lower end of the street, next to the hotel. It can be reached on foot within the city centre. Ask for Quay Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole tower in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the corner windows and rooftop parapet.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the Quay Street pavement just outside the façade, then step back along the street until the whole tower fits. Keep the corner windows and parapet in frame, with the hotel beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines, so the walls do not lean inwards. Hold the phone level at chest height and include a little pavement for scale. Then zoom in for a second shot of the top. Keep the hotel edge to one side rather than centring on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's stonework to focus. If the sky behind it is bright, slide the exposure down a little so the parapet does not wash out. Wipe the lens first, as street photos soon pick up smudges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Quieter pavements make a clean, straight-on shot easier, so try early in the day. In bright sun, check that shadows from the narrow street are not hiding the lower walls.

text.access_note: You photograph it from a public street, but the façade is part of a hotel building, so check the hotel's official site for access details.

name: The Hardiman
label: The Hardiman Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eyre Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Eyre Square' (way/25192080): middle (210 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q140657483: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: The Hardiman is a hotel on Eyre Square, in the centre of Galway. Its stone front is the kind of Victorian frontage that rewards a few steps back, and the lawns and paths of the square give you the space to take it in. The hotel opened on 16 August 1852 as the Railway Hotel. The Midland Great Western Railway built it with money left over from a famine-relief loan used to bring the Athlone to Galway line to completion. John Skipton Mulvany designed it, and the limestone facade was built under the contractor William Dargan. It has had several names since, and took its present one in 2019 from the Galway historian and scholar James Hardiman. For a phone photo, the appeal is the long, regular row of windows and the pale stone against the green of the square. Stand on the open ground in front of the hotel and let the lawn fill the lower part of the picture. That gives a sense of place and keeps passers-by from blocking the building. A very wide shot tends to make the building look small and the sky look empty. Try a slightly tighter view that takes in the full width of the frontage and a little foreground. Take a second frame with the square's paths leading towards the hotel. Treat this as a starting point and adjust the framing once you are there.
text.geographic_location: The Hardiman stands at 14/15 Eyre Square, in Galway city centre, facing the square's lawns. Eyre Square's official name is John F. Kennedy Memorial Park.
text.directions_text: Make your way on foot to Eyre Square in the city centre. From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to the hotel's front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the facade. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole width in, and keep the phone level so the building does not lean. Use 2x if you want to pick out the windows and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Eyre Square. The hotel's stone Victorian facade seen across the square's lawns and paths, from the open ground in front of it. From there the hotel lies to the south-east, and you see its stone Victorian facade across the lawns and paths of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the base of the building up with a lower grid line, leaving the lawn or path in the bottom third. Keep the phone upright and level so the vertical edges of the facade stay straight. Take one wide frame with the square in front and one closer frame of the frontage and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the pale stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the front of the building is evenly lit, such as a bright but overcast day or soft daylight, and avoid harsh shadows across the facade. Early morning is usually quieter on the square.

text.access_note: Eyre Square is an open public park that can be visited on foot, and the hotel is a private business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft, even daylight such as a bright overcast day usually suits a pale stone facade better than harsh shadow.
Early morning is usually quieter on Eyre Square.

name: Tigh Neachtain
label: Tigh Neachtain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cross Street Upper / Quay Street corner' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q137763022: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous colourful pub at Quay Street.

text.description: Tigh Neachtain (often called Naughton's) is a traditional pub on the corner of Quay Street and Cross Street Upper, just off Shop Street, the main pedestrian street in Galway. Its bright blue-and-yellow frontage makes it one of the easiest buildings in the area to spot, and the corner position gives you a nice angled view with both streets leading away from it. The pub opened in 1894. Before that the building was the home of Richard Martin, the animal rights campaigner who founded the original Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, and who belonged to one of the Tribes of Galway, the merchant families who shaped the city for centuries. The name over the door is in Irish, and this once drew the anger of the Black and Tans during the War of Independence. For a phone photo, the colour does most of the work. Stand on the corner in front of the main facade and let the sign, the painted woodwork and any street-side seating fill the frame, with the two approaching streets leading the eye in. It is a busy corner, so people and outdoor tables may drift into the shot. Wait a moment for a gap, or use them to give a sense of the street's life. Quay Street, just along from the corner, gives a second view of the front of the pub seen along the street.
text.geographic_location: In Galway city centre, on the corner of Quay Street and Cross Street Upper, close to Shop Street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so finish on foot in the city centre. Start from Shop Street, the main pedestrian street, and walk to the corner of Quay Street and Cross Street Upper, which is close by. The pub is on the corner and is easy to recognise by its blue-and-yellow front. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole corner in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the pub is directly at your location, so turn to face the building and use the two street approaches to frame it. If you want a different view, walk a short way along Quay Street and look back along the front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the corner of the building with one of the vertical lines so the walls stay straight. Include the sign and the seating, and let the two streets lead into the picture. For an alternative, shoot along Quay Street to show the sign and the front of the building at street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blue paintwork to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the bright colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone upright and keep it level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter, with fewer people and tables in front of the pub. Evening can give a livelier, busier scene if you want that atmosphere.

text.access_note: The outside of the pub is photographed from the public street; check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, as opening times change.

Outdoor seating and passers-by can block the view at busy times.

name: Monument to Christopher Columbus (Galway)
label: Columbus Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Spanish Parade' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/699771692: the OpenStreetMap point 'Christopher Columbus Monument'.

text.description:
The Monument to Christopher Columbus stands on Spanish Parade, right beside the Spanish Arch, with the River Corrib harbour behind it. It is a seabird-shaped bronze sculpture in an open public space, so you can walk around it and choose your angle. That openness, with the old arch and the water close behind, is what makes it easy to photograph.

The memorial was put up in 1992, the year of the Columbus Quincentenary, to mark Columbus's visit to Galway in 1477. The sculpture was commissioned from the Cork artist Mick Wilkins and was a gift from Genoa, Columbus's hometown. The monument is also a subject of debate: it was defaced in June 2020 and some people called for its removal, so it is worth looking at its current condition when you arrive.

For a phone photo, the classic view is from the open space in front of the Spanish Arch, facing the monument, so the sculpture fills the foreground and the arch and harbour sit behind it. Take a few steps to either side until the arch sits beside the sculpture rather than directly behind it. Keep the phone level using the gridlines, and check the edges of the frame for passers-by and signs before you tap the shutter. A quick look at the plinth is also worthwhile, as it carries an inscription you can photograph as a detail shot.
text.geographic_location: In Galway city centre, on Spanish Parade beside the Spanish Arch.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Spanish Arch area in Galway city centre. The monument stands in the open space right beside the arch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the sculpture with the arch and harbour behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the open space and the water. Use 2x if your phone has it for a tighter shot of the bronze shape alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the wider view, step back into the open space in front of the Spanish Arch and face the monument. From there you see the seabird-shaped bronze in the foreground with the Spanish Arch and the River Corrib harbour behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the sculpture off-centre and let the Spanish Arch fill the other side of the frame. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon and the arch straight. Crouching slightly lowers the viewpoint and lifts the bronze against the sky and water. Take a second, closer shot of the plinth inscription.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the sculpture keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, when there are likely to be fewer people around the arch and the open space. Soft light on an overcast day also keeps the bronze from glaring.

text.access_note: It stands in an open public space beside the Spanish Arch, and no access restriction was reported.
